Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty Images Houthis Houthis seize key Yemeni port of Mocha in drive to take control of Red Sea coast Iran and its proxies move closer to full control of two shipping chokepoints as regional conflict widens Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Thu 10 Sep 2026 07.39 EDT Last modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Yemen’s Houthi rebels are making a concerted drive to take full control of the country’s Red Sea coast, claiming control of the key port of Mocha, in the most serious wave of fighting with the Saudi-backed government in years. Seizure of the coast would be a strategic disaster for Saudi Arabia and the US, taking Iran and its proxies closer to full control of two chokepoints for western shipping on opposite sides of the Arabian peninsula: the Bab al-Mandeb at the southern end of the Red Sea and the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. Observers have said a reduction in hostilities – the most intense since the UN-sponsored ceasefire of April 2022 put an end to major military exchanges – now seems unlikely in what is seen as an attempt by the Houthis to open a second front in the Iran-US war, alongside the battle for control of Hormuz. The Royal United Services Institute ( Rusi), a London-based defence and security thinktank, said the situation in Yemen was spiralling out of control, adding that the UN-recognised Yemeni government was opening new fronts against the Houthis in the hope it could put more pressure on the rebels than they could withstand. View image in fullscreen A screengrab from video footage released by Saudi-backed forces shows a rocket being fired during fighting in Taiz province. Photograph: Yemen National Resistance Forces/AFP/Getty Images The fighting has also raised questions about whether Saudi Arabia, which on Thursday launched as many as 40 airstrikes on Houthi targets, will activate the Mecca defence agreement and ask its co-signatories, Pakistan and Turkey, to send forces. The pact is designed to be defensive in nature and believed unlikely to apply to Saudi military activities in Yemen. A map showing the area of Yemen controlled by Houthi rebels By taking control of more of the Red Sea coast south of the port of Hodeidah, the Houthis’ aim is to put pressure on Saudi Arabia and the US to agree a deal that lifts the US blockade on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf. Donald Trump on Wednesday acknowledged he did not expect the war with Iran to end before the US midterm elections at the start of November. The latest phase in the escalation began when Houthis attacked energy installations and southern cities in Saudi Arabia using drones and ballistic missiles. In response, the kingdom’s military forces launched at least 15 strikes between 3 and 7 September. View image in fullscreen The aftermath of Houthi strikes on Mocha last month. The rebel group claims it now controls the port. Photograph: Al Joumhouriya TV/Reuters The conflict data monitor Acled estimated there were 276 fatalities over the five-day period alone. The fighting has continued, with the Houthis claiming control of Mocha in Taiz province, as well as the inland city of Hays and the Khalid ibn al-Walid camp, the largest military base in the region. One Houthi-linked estimate suggested rebel forces had gained control of more than 2,320 sq miles (6,000 sq km) of land. The commander of the Yemeni government forces, Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, admitted he had organised a strategic retreat south of Mocha in order to regroup in a secure location. “The armed forces in the western coast paid a heavy price – martyrs and wounded – over the past days as they confronted the Houthi attack planned by Iran, and supported by it,” he said. View image in fullscreen A satellite image shows smoke billowing from an Aramco oil depot near the Saudi city of Abha after a Houthi attack. Photograph: Planet Labs/AFP/Getty Images Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, continues to take advantage of its air superiority to attack Houthi positions, though government sources acknowledged the rebels’ ground advances along the coast and their missile strikes on the strategic Red Sea islands of Zuqar and Hanish. The clashes have ranged across Yemen, including Ad Dali, al-Bayda, Marib, Shabwah, al-Jawf, Hodeidah, and Taiz. In the initial days of the renewed conflict the Houthis found themselves being forced back in some areas as battles on multiple fronts overstretched their resources and fighter numbers. The Houthis will be hoping political divisions inside the Yemeni government, reflected in a lack of an integrated military, will slowly give them the upper hand. The United Arab Emirates, previously a powerful player in southern Yemen where it backed the separatist forces of the Southern Transitional Council, withdrew its financial and military support at the turn of the year. The southern forces have refused to fight outside their own region. View image in fullscreen A screengrab from video footage released by the Saudi-backed forces shows a fighter firing at Houthi rebels in Taiz province. Photograph: Yemen National Resistance Forces/AFP/Getty Images “ A reduction in hostilities anytime soon seems unlikely, as both sides continue to escalate with the goal of inflicting enough damage to the other side to force a compromise,” said Sherwan Hindreen Ali, a Yemen analyst for Acled. “In terms of military capability, both sides are more equal compared to the immediate period prior to the 2022 ceasefire when the Houthis had the upper hand.” He added: “Fighting will remain focused on the fronts of the Red Sea coast in Hodeidah and Taiz, where both the Houthis and the Saudi Arabia-Yemen government have a vested interest in claiming the whole territory to deprive the other side of effective control of the strait of Bab al-Mandab.” The fighting has contributed to the price of oil rising above $100 a barrel after weeks when it was trading closer to $80. View image in fullscreen A screengrab of video footage reportedly showing Houthi attacks on Saudi-backed forces in al-Jawf province. Photograph: Ansarullah Media Centre/AFP/Getty Images The escalantion to this week’s all-out violence has been a slow process. It began after a senior Houthi delegation from the group, which has long been in a complex alliance with Iran, flew to Tehran for the funeral of the Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei in July, returning in an Iranian plane that the Saudis refused to land in rebel-controlled Sana’a. The Saudis instead bombed the runway, leading the Houthis to announce a Red Sea naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in what the Yemeni rebels described as a blockade for a blockade. The 20 July announcement of the blockade was followed by a strike on Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery on 25 July and on a tanker off Yanbu on 24 August. Saudi Arabia has become reliant on the Red Sea route for trade after Iran throttled shipping through the strait of Hormuz following US-Israeli attacks. https://eturbonews.com/tourism-geopoliti.text: Click here i f you have news to share Tourism cannot afford to become a geopolitical trophy. Trump’s reported interest in Viktor Orbán for UN Secretary-General challenges the UAE’s diplomatic ambitions as Israel’s election, US midterms and Saudi-Iran tensions create uncertainty. What does this power struggle mean for UN Tourism, WTTC, aviation, destination investment, and global tourism cooperation? If playback is interrupted, you can restart it. The battle over who will lead the United Nations is becoming more than a diplomatic contest. For tourism ministers, international organizations, airlines and destinations, it raises a fundamental question: Will global tourism remain a bridge between nations, or become another instrument of geopolitical competition? The geopolitical landscape surrounding the United Arab Emirates’ ambitions at the United Nations may have changed dramatically in just 48 hours. As Israel counts votes in an inconclusive election and Americans prepare for consequential midterm elections, reports that Donald Trump’s administration is encouraging former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán to seek the UN’s top job introduce a potentially disruptive alternative to UAE candidate Lana Nusseibeh. The implications extend far beyond New York. Saudi Arabia, Iran, Israel, Africa, UN Tourism, and the World Travel & Tourism Council (WTTC) all have interests in an increasingly unpredictable international order. But is Washington genuinely changing candidates, or simply strengthening its negotiating position? A New Candidate Changes the Equation Only two days ago, eTurboNews published its investigation, UAE UN Bid, UN Tourism and WTTC: Who Will Shape Tourism? Could the UAE’s UN Ambitions Trigger a Leadership Shake-Up at UN Tourism? That article examined the possibility of two Emirati women leading prominent international institutions: Lana Nusseibeh as United Nations Secretary-General and Shaikha Al Nowais, already serving as Secretary-General of UN Tourism. It also questioned whether the UAE’s growing institutional influence could eventually create political complications for UN Tourism, including speculation about a possible early leadership transition. Now, an entirely new development demands reconsideration. According to reports published October 26, the Trump administration has encouraged former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán to consider becoming the next UN Secretary-General. Reports suggest that Russia and China might be receptive to his candidacy. Orbán, who lost power in Hungary after 16 years, represents a very different vision of international leadership from Nusseibeh. He is closely associated with nationalist politics, opposition to liberal internationalism, restrictive immigration policies, and unusually close relationships with both Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin. His possible candidacy would therefore be more than another diplomatic nomination. It could become a contest over the ideological future of the United Nations. Importantly, reported American encouragement is not the same as a formal US endorsement, and there is no established evidence that Washington previously committed its support to Nusseibeh. The question is not whether Trump has officially withdrawn support from the UAE candidate. No such withdrawal has been established. The question is whether the White House has identified a more politically attractive alternative. Trump Tourism : Join the Fight | Trump Tourism Travel from and to the United States and the industry behind has changed under US President Donald Trump. There are new challenges, expectations, and regulations. How Realistic Are Orbán’s Chances? The next Secretary-General must be recommended by the UN Security Council and appointed by the General Assembly. Each of the five permanent Security Council members can effectively block a candidate. Orbán might find sympathetic governments in Washington, Moscow and Beijing. But acceptance by France and the United Kingdom would be a formidable challenge. His political record, particularly on democratic governance, European unity, Russia and human rights, would likely generate significant opposition. There is also an institutional question: Could someone so closely identified with Trump’s political movement credibly serve as an independent Secretary-General for 193 UN member states? The reported Orbán initiative nevertheless matters because the contest is deadlocked. Former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan has emerged as a leading candidate in informal Security Council polling, while Nusseibeh entered the race only recently. None has yet secured the necessary consensus among the permanent members. Orbán’s prospects currently appear politically difficult rather than impossible. His strongest potential role may be as a negotiating instrument: a candidate Washington can promote to pressure other governments toward a compromise. That remains analysis, not a verified Trump strategy. Israel: An Election Without a Winner Israel’s October 27 election has produced another uncertainty. With votes still being counted on October 28, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party is leading as an individual party, but neither his coalition nor the opposition led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot has established a clear parliamentary majority. The 120-seat Knesset requires a governing majority of 61. Arab-led parties could play an important role in determining the eventual outcome. Coalition negotiations may take weeks. For the UAE, this uncertainty matters. The Abraham Accords have given Abu Dhabi an important relationship with Israel, but that relationship does not automatically translate into Israeli support for an Emirati UN Secretary-General. On October 26, Israeli UN Ambassador Danny Danon praised Nusseibeh’s diplomatic qualifications while explicitly declining to endorse her. Israel, he said, was not publicly supporting any candidate. This distinction is significant. A Netanyahu-led government might favor a UN Secretary-General more sympathetic to Israel’s security concerns. An Eisenkot-led government could change diplomatic tactics without necessarily changing Israel’s fundamental security priorities. Neither scenario guarantees support for Nusseibeh or Orbán. For tourism, a stable Israeli government capable of supporting regional normalization would be far more consequential than the nationality of the next UN chief. United States Midterms: A Weakened Trump Could Become More Unpredictable The November 3 US midterm elections could determine how much political freedom Trump retains during the second half of his presidency. Recent polling suggests significant difficulties for Republicans. A Reuters/Ipsos survey released October 26 put Trump’s approval rating at just 32%. A PBS-reported poll found Democrats leading Republicans by eight percentage points among likely voters. Neither figure guarantees the outcome, particularly in individual Senate and House races. A Democratic takeover of the House would increase congressional scrutiny of Trump’s foreign policy, while Republican losses in the Senate could complicate his domestic agenda. But the UN Secretary-General selection would remain principally an executive-branch diplomatic matter. Congress does not cast America’s Security Council vote. A politically weakened Trump might seek an international victory through a dramatic UN appointment. Alternatively, his administration might become more transactional, seeking concessions from allies before supporting their candidates. For the UAE, both possibilities create uncertainty. Saudi Arabia and Iran: The Real Wild Cards Saudi Arabia’s position is particularly interesting. The Gulf Cooperation Council unanimously endorsed Nusseibeh on October 22, including Saudi Arabia. That remains the official regional position. However, the Saudi government is confronting a much larger strategic problem: Iran. On October 26, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman joined Turkish and Pakistani officials for high-level discussions in Tehran aimed at preventing renewed regional military escalation. The talks followed continuing conflict involving Iran, the United States, Israel and Yemen’s Houthis. Disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, attacks on Saudi infrastructure and threats of further military action have made regional stability an urgent priority. This creates a diplomatic paradox. Saudi Arabia may publicly support an Emirati candidate while prioritizing an international settlement that protects its own security and economic transformation. Riyadh’s Vision 2030 tourism ambitions depend on reliable aviation, investment, energy infrastructure and international confidence. These interests are vulnerable to regional conflict. Iran, meanwhile, has no direct vote in the Security Council’s permanent-member decisions. But Tehran’s relationships with Russia and China could influence the broader diplomatic environment. Would Moscow and Beijing prefer Orbán because of his previous relationships with their governments? Would they instead support a Gulf diplomat with strong regional connections? Or could they seek a compromise candidate? There are no verified answers. The critical distinction is that Saudi Arabia’s official endorsement of Nusseibeh is confirmed; any claim that Riyadh is privately working against her remains unproven. Nusseibeh’s Achievements—and Her Vulnerabilities The UAE candidate should not be underestimated. Nusseibeh served as the UAE’s permanent representative to the UN for more than a decade, helped secure her country’s Security Council membership and developed extensive diplomatic relationships. Her candidacy could also advance the longstanding demand for the United Nations to appoint its first female Secretary-General. These are substantial qualifications. Yet her campaign faces serious scrutiny over allegations concerning UAE support for Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces. The UAE denies the accusations, while human rights organizations have raised questions about Nusseibeh’s previous defence of Emirati policy. The next Secretary-General must be capable of addressing conflicts impartially, including those involving the candidate’s own government. This is a legitimate test of every contender, not a reason to presume guilt. Has the Outlook for UN Tourism and WTTC Dramatically Changed? The answer is yes politically, but not yet institutionally. Our earlier article examined whether Nusseibeh’s possible election might create pressure around Shaikha Al Nowais’s leadership of UN Tourism. Orbán’s emergence makes that hypothetical outcome less certain. If Nusseibeh fails to secure the UN position, the central premise behind speculation about two Emiratis simultaneously leading prominent UN-system organizations disappears. However, Al Nowais’s mandate through 2029 remains unchanged regardless of who wins in New York. There is no confirmed resignation plan or established requirement that she leave. The UAE’s previously announced $15 million pledge to support UN Tourism programs also deserves continued scrutiny, independently of Nusseibeh’s candidacy. Meanwhile, WTTC’s Malta summit highlighted ambitions to expand destination relationships, engage one million tourism SMEs and strengthen cooperation with international institutions. Those initiatives do not depend on an Emirati UN Secretary-General. WTTC may therefore gain importance as a platform connecting businesses and destinations during a period of geopolitical fragmentation. But it cannot replace the intergovernmental legitimacy of UN Tourism simply through commercial reach. The bigger fear is that global tourism governance becomes fragmented between governments pursuing diplomatic prestige and private institutions pursuing influence. The bigger opportunity is to create measurable cooperation on aviation connectivity, crisis response, investment, sustainability and small-business participation. Three Possible Outcomes Scenario 1: Nusseibeh wins The UAE achieves an extraordinary diplomatic victory. Questions about its international influence intensify, but UN Tourism’s leadership remains legally independent. Scenario 2: Orbán wins Trump secures a symbolic ideological victory. However, opposition from Western governments makes this outcome difficult, and the UN could face further political polarization. Scenario 3: A compromise candidate emerges Deadlock produces a broadly acceptable candidate, potentially Grynspan or another contender. Neither Trump’s reported preference nor the UAE’s ambitions prevail completely. This remains a plausible diplomatic outcome. Opinion: Tourism Cannot Afford to Become a Geopolitical Trophy The most important development may not be Orbán’s candidacy itself. It is the growing possibility that leadership of the United Nations becomes another instrument in great-power competition. For global tourism, this is dangerous. Destinations require peace, predictable aviation routes, open borders, investment confidence and international cooperation. They cannot build sustainable visitor economies around shifting political alliances. The UAE has demonstrated considerable diplomatic ambition. Saudi Arabia is increasingly central to regional security and tourism investment. Israel’s next government will influence the future of normalization. Iran’s confrontation with Washington and its neighbors threatens the wider travel economy. And Trump’s midterm political fortunes could influence how aggressively Washington pursues its preferred international leadership. The earlier eTurboNews investigation remains relevant, but its central scenario has become more uncertain. What has dramatically changed is not who controls UN Tourism. It is the probability that the wider diplomatic environment will determine which international ambitions succeed. The next UN Secretary-General should not be chosen as a reward for geopolitical loyalty, a victory for one regional power, or a symbol of ideological conquest. And global tourism should not wait for that decision to determine its future. The industry needs functioning institutions, accountable leadership, and peace more than it needs another powerful title. Tourism: A Geopolitical Trophy? Update Live Coverage Tourism cannot afford to become a geopolitical trophy. Its institutions must serve destinations, businesses, and communities—not the political ambitions of whichever government succeeds in placing its candidate at the top.” You may also like About the author Juergen T Steinmetz Juergen Thomas Steinmetz is a global tourism leader, media entrepreneur, and veteran journalist with 40+ years of industry experience.
